elements.text: Killer of Men follows Mace, an enslaved man forced into mandingo fights. After killing an opponent, he stumbles upon the burial of the man he killed, igniting a reckoning with guilt, faith, and the violence shaping his life and identity.

Mace fights because the alternative is the field, and then the ground. On a South Carolina plantation in 1834 his owner stages bouts against other enslaved men and takes the wagers; Mace has never lost, and every win buys him another season.

Then a fight ends in a death, and he follows the body to a burial held in secret in the Yoruba faith he was born to. The rites are for a man he killed. An elder tells him what he would have been across the water, and he sees, for the first time, what he has become.

K I L L E R   O F   M E N
D I R E C T O R ' S   S T A T E M E N T

Growing up, I was always one of the youngest in my year, but my height made me one of the tallest in the class. I was often one of the biggest in the room. As I got older, I started noticing how my mere presence was often seen as either a point of praise or persecution. My physicality, tied so closely to my skin, made me seem more menacing, more dangerous than the other boys—even those bigger and stronger than I was. It’s never anything overt, but small, incessant microaggressions. Death by a 1000 needles. It’s a plight that’s shaped me throughout my life, leaving me hyper-aware of myself in spaces. This experience, this reality, is tied to the plight of the Black man in America.

The concept of Mandingo fighting has always fascinated me. It’s a strange, bastardized idea in media and literature. To me, it represents many things: the commercialization of sports and entertainment, the myth of Black-on-Black crime, the portrayal of savagery in history, and the media. It’s always been used to showcase the “Black brute,” but it has never been shown subjectively from the perspective of those involved. What are their lives like? What do they hold dear? What keeps a man going when he’s put in a situation like that?

Setting this film in slavery times, rather than in the present day or during the 1960s, allows me to examine the deep-rooted history of this aggression. Visually, I want the fight scenes to reflect the physical sports Black men often participate in—body slams, boxing, football tackles—to show history repeating itself through various forms of expression.

By setting the story in the 1800s, I also had the chance to explore my heritage. With slavery still in full force and new enslaved people being brought in from Africa, I can examine the past in different ways.
I want to delve into the spirituality of the enslaved at the time, capturing the mix of cultures, beliefs, and religions that slowly formed what we now know as Black culture.

Killer of Men is an expression of pain—absolute brutality and suffering. But it’s also a story of resilience, culture, and spirituality. This story has kept me awake at night, terrified of what I’m putting on the screen.

Killer of Men has been a grueling process—one that’s forced me to question a lot of myself as a man and as a storyteller. This is my Oriki, my folktale, my poem. I won’t shy away from telling difficult stories or giving a voice to the voiceless. I will honor my ancestors and my culture in everything I do.
F I L M M A K E R S

Jordan Betine is a Nigerian-American filmmaker raised between Lagos, Nigeria, and Ashburn, Virginia. He earned his undergraduate degree in film from Howard University. Jordan studied Directing at the American Film Institute, where he directed six short films across genres, including historical drama, social realism, and surrealist comedy. His thesis film, "Killer of Men," is a historical drama set in 1830s South Carolina about an enslaved man who is forced into underground prizefighting. His work explores power, identity, and the African diaspora.

Ruoxiao Li is a storyteller from China. A graduate of the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, she is currently pursuing a degree in Producing at the American Film Institute. She is mentored by Lianne Halfon, whose notable works include Juno and Ghost World.

Luke Scroggins studied theater under David Connelly at the North East School of the Arts in his home town of San Antonio and continued at Otterbein University School of Theatre, earning a BFA in Acting. Television credits include SWITCHED AT BIRTH, GENERAL HOSPITAL and DAYS OF OUR LIVES. After a period coordinating and editing for fashion clients, Scroggins joined the Dark Side and began working in camera. Recently he has moved into the narrative space as Utility on the independent feature FRESH KILLS and the limited series RZR. He made his cinematographer debut on the short films COSMIC BEACH and L'DIRECTOR

Rajarajeshwari "RJ" Ragampudi, is a recent graduate with a bachelor's degree in Architecture from India. She is recognized in her university for her undergraduate thesis, an in-depth research-based design project through the study of the films of the Indian film director, Satyajit Ray. Her experience as an Architect has helped her gain practical knowledge in spatial design, construction and project management. Along with this, she is also skilled in creative visualization with a stark interest in Film, enabling her to pursue an MFA degree in Production Design. She strives to design sets that are not only authentic to the setting but deeply character-driven, enhancing and punctuating key moments in the story.

You Wu is a working editor with four years of professional experience. He has worked on a range of short films across different genres, contributing as both an editor and in key roles such as DIT and sound designer. Several of the films he edited have been selected for major film festivals, including LA Shorts and the Avignon International Film Festival.

Erik Orjiako is a Swedish-born Nigerian American actor and writer based in Los Angeles. He studied English and communications at UMass Amherst and earned an MFA in screenwriting at the New York Film Academy. A graduate of Second City Hollywood's improv program, he has performed with its sketch team and written shows there. His credits include the series Minx, the short film Al Davis: Just Win Baby and the podcast series The Imperfection. He has also worked as a script reader and creative executive. In Killer of Men he plays Mace.

Eric Pargac is a Los Angeles-based actor and filmmaker who grew up in Texas. He was a founding artistic director of Furious Theatre Company in Los Angeles, where he performed in ten productions and shared StageSceneLA's 2006-2007 Lead Actor of the Year (Drama) award for An Impending Rupture of the Belly. He has also performed at Artists Repertory Theatre in Portland, Intiman Theatre in Seattle and the IRT Theater in New York. His television credits include The Late Show with Stephen Colbert and HBO's Succession. He starred in, co-directed and co-produced the web series The Digressions. He is a member of SAG-AFTRA and Actors' Equity. In Killer of Men he plays Master Kenner.

Jamal Dennis is a Los Angeles-based actor and stunt performer. His training includes technique and scene study at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art and scene study with Lesly Kahn and Craig Archibald. He holds a black belt in martial arts and has trained in Kyokushin, Wushu, Ninjutsu and Shotokan. He played the lead, Lavelle Sanders, in the series Be Someone. His screen credits include The Young and the Restless, S.W.A.T., Marvel's Runaways, Zoo, Mississippi Grind and Glory Road, and he has performed stunts on Sinners, Emancipation and Grudge Match. He is a member of SAG-AFTRA. In Killer of Men he plays Kojo.

Sandra McDaniels is a Los Angeles-based actress and a member of SAG-AFTRA. Her screen credits include the Apple TV+ series Truth Be Told, the short films Providence and 172 Push-Ups, and the film Gingersnap Christmas, in which she plays Gramma Belle. In Killer of Men she plays the Elder.
